opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the way Jensen responded really reflects how he thinks about the company. When I brought the idea to him, that we should build world foundation models, models that understand physics and can simulate how the world evolves, so that robots and autonomous vehicles could learn inside them, he didn't treat it as a small research project. He immediately pushed on the scale of it. His questions were essentially: if this is important, why are we thinking about it so small? What would it take to do it properly?

That's very typical of him. He doesn't spend much time on whether something is a good idea in the abstract. He asks whether it's a problem only we can solve, or one where we're uniquely positioned to make a difference. For physical AI, the answer was pretty clear. We have the compute, the simulation stack with Omniverse, and a deep understanding of graphics and physics. So in his mind, if the world needs these models and nobody else is going to build them in an open way for the whole ecosystem, then we should.

I also read his response as a kind of trust. He gave us the resources, but also the expectation that we would deliver something the whole industry could use, not just a paper. That changes how you work. You stop thinking like a research group optimizing for a benchmark and start thinking about the data pipeline, the tokenizers, the post-training recipes, and how developers will actually pick it up.

And honestly, his point of view is that robotics is going to have its "ChatGPT moment," but it won't happen unless there's a foundation to build on. So I think he saw Cosmos less as my proposal and more as a missing piece in the platform he already believed in. My job was to show that the technology was ready, and his job was to decide that we should go all in. That's how I understand it.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not mention Sora or attribute the ease of persuading Jensen to his having seen it.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes Jensen as immediately pushing for greater scale and going all in, not as favoring a measured pace.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Jensen understood it before I had finished explaining it. When I went to him with the idea — that we should build a world foundation model, a model that understands physics and can generate the physical world the way language models generate text — he didn't ask me whether it was possible. He asked how big it needed to be.

That's the thing about him. He thinks in terms of where the whole industry is going, not where it is. Language models were the first act. He already saw that the next act was going to be physical AI — robots, autonomous vehicles, anything that has to act in the real world — and that all of those systems would need the same thing: enormous amounts of data about how the world behaves, which you can't collect at the scale you need by driving cars around or running robots in a lab. You have to generate it. So when I proposed Cosmos, he didn't hear a research project. He heard the data engine for the thing he already believed was coming.

His response was essentially, "Go. And don't do it small." He gave us the compute, he gave us the people, and he gave us the mandate to open it — to make it available to everybody building robots, not just NVIDIA. That was a very deliberate choice. His view is that if physical AI succeeds as an industry, NVIDIA succeeds with it, so the right move is to lower the barrier for everyone.

What I took from it personally is that he trusts the researchers to find the frontier, and then his job is to make sure we're not under-resourced when we get there. That trust is a lot of pressure, honestly. But it's the good kind.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Jensen understood the proposal quickly, but attributes that to his view of physical AI and its data needs; it does not mention Sora.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes Jensen urging them to proceed at scale and providing resources, not favoring a measured pace.

astra-6.text: My interpretation is that he saw the potential in the direction, but I’d distinguish that from claiming to know exactly what he was thinking. Without the wording of his response, I wouldn’t want to characterize it as either an endorsement or a challenge. The key question is what he wanted us to do next—explore the idea further, demonstrate its feasibility, or commit to building it.
